## Conclusion: Your skepticism is well supported by the evidence

Current evidence does **not** show that whole-body vibration (WBV) therapy directly prevents fractures in people with osteoporosis. Here's the breakdown:

**No direct fracture-prevention evidence.** The most relevant meta-analysis on this exact question—a 2017 systematic review/meta-analysis in *BMJ Open* pooling randomized controlled trials in adults over 50—found WBV had **no significant effect on actual fracture incidence**, concluding "the impact of WBV on fractures requires further larger adequately powered studies" ([bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342](https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342)). No trial has been powered with fracture as a primary endpoint, so causal claims about fracture prevention remain unproven.

**Bone density results are inconsistent, and a rigorous trial found no benefit.** A well-conducted 12-month randomized trial published in *Annals of Internal Medicine* found that WBV therapy (at two different vibration protocols) **did not improve bone mineral density or bone structure** in postmenopausal women already receiving calcium/vitamin D ([acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/0003-4819-155-10-201111150-00005](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/0003-4819-155-10-201111150-00005)). Other reviews report mixed or modest density gains, but effect sizes are small and heterogeneous across studies.

**Modest indirect benefit only via fall reduction.** The BMJ Open meta-analysis did find WBV reduced fall rates, and falls are a major cause of fragility fractures — so WBV may offer indirect protective value through improved balance/strength rather than through strengthening bone itself.

**Bottom line:** WBV is not a proven fracture-prevention therapy for osteoporosis. Any benefit appears to run through fall reduction rather than bone strengthening, and larger, fracture-focused trials are still needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.
